outputs.L1:
Paul lost his footing and executed a spectacular corkscrew. It looked as though he were acting out a series of renga in the air. The general theme was prevenient grace. But the white rim broke his form, and he struck the bathwater like the great charred bough of a tree. A semicircle of his shoes—Oxfords, monk straps, bluchers, a lone boot—crowded in to get a look.

After that, Morphy was only surface. You can look into anything and see what you want. Pierre, for example, swore he could read stock returns in the little channels of Morphy’s pruned thumbs. He even called in Schiaparelli’s niece. She entered with a shoe on her head, I swear. There are pictures—look it up.

My uncle, my unfortunate uncle, says the whole event—Morphy in the tub—looked floral, with shoes for petals. Just to be difficult, I said, “A saucer of milk”: a teacup on a dish, alone in the quiet, waiting for a cougar to come by. I always bank on something parched and ambling to make my point. Or else on something with a broken heel, covered in wet newspaper and huddled beside the highway. All thumbs.
outputs.L2:
Paul slipped and spun through an astonishing corkscrew, as though performing a chain of renga in midair, all of them concerned with prevenient grace. Then the tub’s white edge disrupted the composition, and he crashed into the bathwater like a large, fire-blackened tree limb. His footwear—Oxfords, monk straps, bluchers, and one solitary boot—gathered in a half circle to watch.

From then on, Morphy existed only as a surface, and any surface can reflect whatever the observer hopes to find. Pierre, for instance, insisted that the tiny grooves in Morphy’s trimmed thumbs revealed stock-market returns. He even summoned Schiaparelli’s niece, who arrived, I swear, wearing a shoe as a hat. Photographs exist; you can verify it.

My poor uncle claims that the entire scene—Morphy lying in the bathtub—resembled a flower, with shoes forming its petals. Purely to be contrary, I called it a “saucer of milk”: a teacup resting by itself on a plate in the stillness, awaiting the arrival of a cougar. To support an argument, I invariably rely on some dried-out creature wandering along—or, alternatively, on something with a snapped heel, wrapped in soggy newspaper and curled beside the highway. Nothing but thumbs.
outputs.L3:
Paul loses his footing and spirals helplessly through the air before crashing into the water of the bathtub. In the aftermath, a semicircle of assorted shoes gathers around the tub, arranged like silent spectators observing the strange accident.

Morphy then becomes less a person than a surface onto which those present project their own meanings. Pierre claims that the channels of Morphy’s pruned thumbs reveal stock-market returns, and he even summons Schiaparelli’s eccentric niece to examine them. The narrator and his uncle interpret the spectacle differently: one imagines the shoes as petals forming an enormous flower around the tub, while the other sees the bath as a saucer of milk set out in anticipation of a cougar. Together, these contrasting images transform the fall into a surreal scene shaped as much by the observers’ imaginations as by what has actually happened.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents Paul Morphy’s fall into a bathtub as more than a simple accident. Rather than narrating the event in a clear, chronological manner, it breaks the scene into disconnected images, uncertain explanations, and surreal associations. Shoes, flowers, omens, and stranded animals appear around Morphy without settling into a single coherent pattern. Each detail seems to promise an explanation, yet every possible meaning is displaced by another. The result is a dreamlike atmosphere in which ordinary objects become symbols and physical reality is continually reshaped by imagination.

Morphy himself remains strangely passive at the center of this interpretive activity. His fall exposes him as vulnerable, but the poem does not grant him a stable voice or a definitive account of what happened. Instead, those who witness or contemplate the incident project their own fears, desires, superstitions, and private associations onto him. One observer may treat the shoes as evidence, another may read the flowers as signs of beauty or death, while someone else may understand the event as an omen. The stranded animals deepen the sense of helplessness and displacement, reflecting Morphy’s own condition while also opening the scene to increasingly remote interpretations.

This accumulation of meanings turns Morphy into a blank surface. He is less a fully explained individual than a figure through whom others attempt to organize an unsettling event. Because the accident resists a single interpretation, the observers compensate by inventing narratives that make it seem purposeful or symbolic. Their explanations reveal more about themselves than about Morphy. What begins as a moment of bodily instability becomes an occasion for psychological and imaginative projection.

The poem therefore explores the distance between an event and the stories created around it. A fall may be accidental, embarrassing, or painful, but perception transforms it into a sign charged with hidden significance. Through fragmented language and competing images, the poem refuses to decide which interpretation is correct. Morphy’s vulnerability remains real, yet it is almost obscured by the elaborate meanings imposed upon it. In this way, the poem suggests that human beings rarely encounter accidents directly: they turn them into symbols, omens, and personal narratives in order to manage the uncertainty those accidents expose.
outputs.L5: Paul stood at the edge of the forest, holding an old map. The path ahead looked dark and uncertain. But he refused to turn back. Somewhere beyond the trees, he believed, a new adventure was waiting for him.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about a man named Paul Morphy falling into a bathtub, incorporating shoes, prevenient grace, stock returns, Schiaparelli’s niece, and a cougar.
counterfactuals.output:
Paul Morphy fell into the bathtub at noon, still wearing his shoes, and the water rose around him like an audience that had forgotten how to applaud. On the tiles, black and white squares softened into fog. Each faucet whispered a different opening; each bar of soap declined to be king.

Prevenient grace had arrived a moment earlier, disguised as a hotel attendant carrying towels. It left without knocking, certain Paul would fall exactly where mercy had already placed the water.

From the drain came news of stock returns: railroads ascending, sugar collapsing, a modest dividend declared by the moon. Paul listened gravely. His shoes filled with bubbles and began to speculate against gravity.

Then Schiaparelli’s niece entered in a hat shaped like an eclipse. She carried a small red ladder and said, “Uncle has discovered canals on your forehead.” Behind her padded a cougar, golden and soundless, with the patient eyes of a creditor. It drank from the tub, lapping up whole gambits, whole years, the little drowned certificates of profit.

Paul moved a rook beneath the foam. The cougar purred. Somewhere, markets closed like exhausted flowers.

“Check,” said Schiaparelli’s niece.

But grace, having preceded them all, had already removed the king.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an absurdist literary passage in which a spectacular fall becomes variously interpreted as poetry, theology, flowers, divination, and a saucer of milk.
counterfactuals.output:
At noon, the Minister of Elevations stepped from the highest balcony and fell through thirteen awnings, a flock of municipal pigeons, and the final chord of a brass band.

The poets applauded first. They declared the descent a new form of verse: long, vertical, and impossible to revise. His hat, arriving several seconds later, was praised as the perfect last line.

The theologians objected. This was no poem, they said, but a sermon on gravity, delivered without notes. The broken awnings represented the veils of ignorance; the pigeons, naturally, were minor angels; the brass band was doctrinally unfortunate but perhaps necessary.

By evening, flowers had sprung from every place he had struck: red geraniums from the first awning, white lilies from the second, and from the third a single black tulip that refused all questions. Botanists called it an unprecedented bloom. Florists tied ribbons around the evidence.

The diviners came at dusk. They studied the arrangement of petals, feathers, brass buttons, and one surviving shoe. From these they predicted seven years of ladders, a marriage between two thunderstorms, and the assassination of a clock by its own hands.

Only the old woman who kept the café remained unimpressed. She gathered the Minister’s hat, dusted it carefully, and set it upside down beside the door. Then she poured into it a saucer’s worth of milk.

“For the cat,” she explained.

There was no cat, but by midnight the moon had climbed down from the sky and begun to drink.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, dreamlike prose poem about an unfortunate uncle in a bathtub, using fragmented spacing, strange similes, dark humor, and unreliable narration.
counterfactuals.output:
Uncle Vargo in the bathtub again—  
or for the first time, depending  
which wall is remembering—

knees pale as two loaves  
the baker drowned before dawn,  
moustache afloat, a small black republic  
declaring independence from his face.

He says the water is fine.

There is no water.

There are only taps, coughing rust,  
and a blue depth where the porcelain  
has forgotten its name.

                           Uncle, we say,  
                           pass the soap.

He hands us a pocket watch, warm and ticking  
like a beetle employed by the government.

Outside, noon hangs crooked.  
A hearse reverses through the roses.  
Someone laughs in the medicine cabinet—  
possibly my mother,  
possibly the razor learning to speak.

Uncle Vargo has always been unfortunate.  
Once he married a staircase.  
Once he swallowed Thursday  
and spent seven years apologizing to clocks.  
Once—though I may be inventing this—  
he died of a minor misunderstanding  
with a swan.

Now his toes rise through the steam,  
ten blunt prophets  
predicting absolutely nothing.

                           The plug chain coils  
                           at his wrist  
                           like a silver excuse.

We ask if he needs help.

No, no, he says,  
I am merely sinking upward.

Then the tub begins filling  
with black feathers, unpaid bills,  
the smell of hospitals after rain.  
His smile slips sideways,  
a portrait poorly nailed.

I remember pulling him out.

I remember pushing him in.

I was not born yet.

By evening the bath is empty  
except for his hat,  
three minnows,  
and a note in my handwriting:

                           DEAR FAMILY,  
                           THE UNCLE HAS BEEN CANCELLED  
                           DUE TO WEATHER.

We serve cake at the funeral.  
It tastes like wet plaster  
and everyone asks for seconds.

Upstairs, behind the locked bathroom door,  
the taps applaud softly.

Uncle Vargo sings from the drain—

                           or the pipes sing him—

thin, cheerful, impossible,  
like a man whistling  
while falling through his own obituary.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental monologue inspired by contemporary surrealist poetry. Include Oxfords, monk straps, bluchers, renga, pruned thumbs, wet newspaper, and the phrase “All thumbs.”
counterfactuals.output:
I wake beneath a table set for weather.  
The forks are lightning; the plate keeps turning  
its pale face away.

By the door: Oxfords, monk straps, bluchers—  
three species of obedient animal  
waiting to be filled with departure.

But I have misplaced my feet.

I search the sink, where a wet newspaper  
has learned to whisper through its teeth.  
Yesterday dissolves around the headlines.  
My pruned thumbs drift in the basin  
like two exhausted kings.

“All thumbs,” says the mirror.

It has no mouth, only a small red staircase  
climbing into my reflection.

I begin a renga with the radiator:

*Winter rents a room—*

It answers in knocks,  
each pipe passing the moon  
to another pipe.

*Someone irons the fog.*

Now the shoes are circling me.  
The Oxfords demand grammar.  
The monk straps kneel and unbuckle the hour.  
The bluchers, less devout, drink rain  
from the carpet’s dark acreage.

Listen: I am not alone in this body.  
A committee of moths votes behind my ribs.  
The motion carries.

I put on the wet newspaper.  
I button the drowned advertisements  
to my throat.

Outside, the street opens its enormous drawer,  
and every house lies down inside it—  
neatly, silently,  
beside the missing feet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a bizarre ekphrastic-style paragraph describing “Morphy in the tub,” with shoes gathered like spectators or flower petals and several narrators disagreeing about what the scene resembles.
counterfactuals.output: Morphy sits in the tub as if steeping himself into a new species, knees pale above the water, while shoes gather along the enamel rim—loafers, pumps, one exhausted boot—like spectators awaiting a dive, or petals shaken from a mechanical chrysanthemum. “It resembles a coronation,” says the first narrator, noting the soap crown slipping over his ear. “No, a shipwreck,” insists the second, because every shoelace points toward him like drowning rigging. A third claims it is plainly a garden: Morphy the damp bulb, the faucets silver insects, the shoes in bloom. From somewhere beneath the floorboards, a fourth voice calls it breakfast, though no one can explain why, and Morphy, lifting one wrinkled hand, declares that the scene resembles nothing so much as a committee trying to remember the shape of rain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
